content: Secondary amenorrhea is a condition in which a woman who previously had regular menstrual cycles stops having periods for six months or longer. Amenorrhea refers to the absence of a monthly menstrual cycle. Symptoms of Secondary Amenorrhea: The primary symptom is the absence of menstrual periods for six months or more. The individual must have previously experienced one or more spontaneous menstrual cycles. Additional symptoms that may accompany secondary amenorrhea include: Changes in breast size. Significant weight gain or weight loss. Milk-like discharge from the breasts (galactorrhea). Persistent headaches. Excessive hair growth in areas typical of male patterns (hirsutism) and acne. Vaginal dryness. Changes in voice, such as deepening. If the amenorrhea is caused by a pituitary tumor, symptoms such as vision loss may also occur. Causes of Secondary Amenorrhea: Women who are pregnant, breastfeeding, or in menopause are not classified as having secondary amenorrhea. Hormonal contraceptives, such as birth control pills or Depo-Provera injections, can suppress menstrual bleeding. After discontinuing these methods, it may take more than six months for periods to resume. Risk factors for secondary amenorrhea include: Obesity. Excessive and prolonged physical exercise. Having body fat levels below 15–17%. Severe emotional stress or anxiety. Rapid and significant weight loss, such as from strict dieting or bariatric surgery. Other potential causes include: Pituitary tumors in the brain. Polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS). Premature ovarian failure. Thyroid dysfunction (e.g., hypothyroidism or hyperthyroidism). Certain medications can also lead to missed periods, including: Busulfan. Chemotherapy agents used to treat cancer. Chlorambucil. Cyclophosphamide. Phenothiazines. High-Risk Factors: Medical procedures such as dilation and curettage (D&C) can result in the formation of scar tissue within the uterus, leading to a condition known as Asherman syndrome, which can cause menstruation to stop. Severe pelvic infections may also lead to uterine scarring and cessation of menstruation. When to Seek Medical Attention: It is important to schedule an appointment with a primary care provider or OB/GYN if you have missed more than one menstrual period. Early diagnosis and treatment are essential. Diagnostic Process: A thorough physical examination and pelvic exam are necessary to rule out pregnancy. A pregnancy test will be conducted. Blood tests may be ordered to evaluate hormone levels, including: Estradiol. Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH). Luteinizing hormone (LH). Prolactin. Testosterone. Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Additional diagnostic tests may include: CT scan of the head. MRI of the head. Ultrasound of the pelvis or hysterosonogram. Endometrial biopsy. Genetic testing. Treatment Options: Treatment is determined by the underlying cause of the amenorrhea. In most cases, normal menstrual cycles resume once the primary condition is addressed. For example: If hypothyroidism is the cause, treatment with thyroid hormone supplements will resolve the amenorrhea. If obesity, excessive exercise, or significant weight loss is the cause, treatment may involve modifying exercise routines or achieving weight control. Prognosis: The prognosis depends on the underlying cause of the amenorrhea. Most conditions that lead to secondary amenorrhea respond well to appropriate treatment. Potential Complications: Complications vary depending on the cause of the amenorrhea. In some cases, amenorrhea may be harmless. However, it can also be associated with the overgrowth of the uterine lining (endometrial hyperplasia), which may increase the risk of uterine cancer. Other complications may arise depending on the specific cause of the condition.
